proposal.title: Gradient Descent: A Ball Stepping Down a Loss Surface
proposal.description: A long, narrow bowl-shaped surface with contour lines stands for a loss surface, and a ball sits on its slope. Each time the scene steps, the ball moves a jump downhill. The jump size is the learning rate times the slope where the ball is standing. The ball leaves a path, so you can see whether it slides smoothly to the bottom, zig-zags across the narrow valley, or overshoots and flies off when steps are too large. An arrow on the ball shows the next step before it is taken.

input.request: a ball rolling down a loss surface, step by step

interactions: Press step to move the ball one jump downhill, or let it play to watch many steps in a row.
Change the learning rate: small values give a slow, smooth path; values near 0.3 to 0.5 zig-zag across the narrow valley; values above 0.5 overshoot more each step, and the ball runs off the surface.
Drag the ball to a new starting point on the surface. Its path starts again from there.
Use Clear path to erase the drawn path and keep the ball where it is.
Watch the readouts: step count, current loss (height) and slope steepness.
notices: Changed: the trail draws 100 markers, one every 2 steps, instead of 200; every step still runs.

proposal.original_request: a ball rolling down a loss surface, step by step
proposal.prompt: A long, narrow bowl-shaped surface with contour lines stands for a loss surface, and a ball sits on its slope. Each time the scene steps, the ball moves a jump downhill. The jump size is the learning rate times the slope where the ball is standing. The ball leaves a path, so you can see whether it slides smoothly to the bottom, zig-zags across the narrow valley, or overshoots and flies off when steps are too large. An arrow on the ball shows the next step before it is taken.
requirements: Recommended: experiment. You can step through the descent one jump at a time, change the learning rate and starting point, and compare paths. This shows directly how step size decides whether descent settles, zig-zags or blows up.
Interaction: Press step to move the ball one jump downhill, or let it play to watch many steps in a row.

Interaction: Change the learning rate: small values give a slow, smooth path; values near 0.3 to 0.5 zig-zag across the narrow valley; values above 0.5 overshoot more each step, and the ball runs off the surface.
Interaction: Drag the ball to a new starting point on the surface. Its path starts again from there.
Interaction: Use Clear path to erase the drawn path and keep the ball where it is.
Interaction: Watch the readouts: step count, current loss (height) and slope steepness.
Parameter: Learning rate (step size), 0.02 to 0.6, default 0.1
Goal: Gradient descent repeatedly steps opposite the slope, and the learning rate decides whether the steps settle at the minimum, zig-zag, or diverge.
assumptions: Illustration: the bowl is a made-up loss function, not a trained model's real loss.
The loss is half of (x² + 4y²), a bowl four times steeper across than along its length, with its lowest point at the centre.
Each step is plain gradient descent: the new position is the old position minus the learning rate times the gradient (the slope direction). There is no momentum and no noise.
The ball jumps from point to point. It does not roll with speed or inertia, and it always sits on the surface.
The arrow shows the next step: it points downhill, opposite the gradient, and its length is the learning rate times the gradient.
The trail draws one marker every 2 steps, at most 100 markers; every step still runs.
limitations: Changed: the trail draws 100 markers, one every 2 steps, instead of 200; every step still runs.
Real loss surfaces have millions of dimensions and many dips. This one has two directions and a single lowest point, so the ball cannot get stuck in a local dip.
Descent stops after 200 steps, when the slope is almost flat, or when the ball leaves the drawn square. When it leaves, the readout says it diverged (blew up).

On this bowl, any learning rate below 0.5 eventually reaches the bottom. Loss can still rise for a step while the ball is zig-zagging only if a different surface were used. Here each step lowers the loss when the rate is below 0.5.
